name: Mondelez: When the Consumer Finally Flinches
deck: Mondelez grew revenue 4.3% in 2025 while earnings stayed flat — cocoa prices spiked to 40-year highs and consumers hit the price ceiling on affordable treats. The company proved that commodity cost pass-through stops where consumer income stops.
core_bet: Mondelez is the clearest evidence that commodity cost pass-through has a hard floor: consumer affordability. FY2025 numbers show the mechanism breaking: $38.537B in revenue with 4.3% organic growth should produce EPS expansion, but adjusted EPS held flat at $2.92 because unprecedented cocoa costs consumed all margin gains. Volume/mix collapsed -3.7% even as prices rose, meaning Mondelez raised prices and sold fewer units — the textbook sign of hitting the consumer's willingness to pay. Q1 and Q2 2026 show the company still fighting: volume/mix only recently turned positive at +0.7% in Q2 despite aggressive brand investment. Mondelez is not broken; rather, it exposes the structural limit of the transfer model: when commodity shocks hit, and when consumers are already stretched on discretionary spending, companies absorb the hit instead of passing it through.

mechanism: For three decades, Mondelez and peers built a reliable system: commodity costs rose → raise retail prices → consumers absorb cost → margins preserved. This worked because snacks are low-ticket items ($1.50-$3.00), brand switching costs are real (Oreos, Cadbury, Ritz command shelf space), and consumers didn't notice incremental price creep. In 2024-2025, cocoa prices hit 40-year highs due to supply shocks in Ivory Coast and Ghana, climate stress, and financial speculation. This wasn't gradual — it was a jolt. Mondelez had two choices: absorb the hit to margins or push price through to consumers. Management chose price, and the consumer response was immediate and measurable.

The magnitude is written in Mondelez's own numbers. FY2025: $38.537B revenue, +4.3% organic growth, but adjusted EPS at $2.92 — completely flat from prior year. That is not how revenue growth works. Revenue growth compounds into earnings growth. When it doesn't, commodities are eating the margin. To be explicit: if a company grew revenue 4.3% and nothing else changed, EPS should rise at least 5-7%. Mondelez's stayed flat. Free cash flow was also flat at $3.2B despite $38.5B revenue. Management's own words confirmed the diagnosis: they called 2025 'dynamic and challenging' and cited 'unprecedented cocoa cost headwinds materially pressuring profitability.' Not 'our brand is strong' — profitability was pressured.

The follow-up quarters show the limits more clearly. Q2 2026: $9.355B revenue, +2.2% organic, but volume/mix only +0.7% — still fighting to restore unit sales nine months later. Management had to walk 2026 guidance down: from the historical mid-to-high single digit EPS growth to flat to 5% in constant currency. That guidance floor is a signal of capitulation. Mondelez spent 2026 H1 on brand investment, structural cost cuts, and stabilizing cocoa exposure because price pass-through was exhausted. A company that can no longer rely on price to drive earnings is a company that has hit the affordability ceiling.
why_now: Three shifts broke the model between 2023 and 2025. First, cocoa prices: from roughly $2,500/tonne in 2023 to $5,000+ in 2024-2025 — a shock not gradual drift. Supply disruptions in West Africa (disease, climate, political tension), combined with financial speculation, created a supply squeeze that consumers of cocoa products couldn't avoid or substitute. Second, household budgetary pressure: inflation in the U.S. and Europe from 2022-2023 ate into discretionary spending, especially for lower-income households that form Mondelez's core customer base. Groceries, energy, and rent absorbed the budget first; snack budgets were next to cut. Third, retail dynamics: private-label snacks and value brands gained shelf visibility as consumers actively traded down. That's different from passive acceptance of price — households were actively switching to save $0.25 on a pack of crackers. Mondelez's brands (Oreos, Cadbury, Ritz, LU) are strong, but not so strong they override a 30-cent price gap when household budgets are tight.
who_pays: The direct payer is the consumer: the household that used to buy Oreos every week but now buys every other week, or switches to store-brand. That consumer loses the treat frequency they expected. The household impact is sharper for lower-income families where $0.50 price increase on a snack item matters. Secondary payers are retailers, who watch snack aisles become harder to move unless they feature value-priced private label, which cannibalizes Mondelez shelf space. The third layer is Mondelez's supply chain: farmers, cocoa processors, and logistics partners who signed on assuming Mondelez would pass costs through but now face margin pressure because pass-through stopped. A cocoa farmer in Ghana negotiated supply contracts on cocoa prices at $3,000/tonne; when those prices doubled, the farmer expected Mondelez to pass it through. Instead, Mondelez absorbed it, and the farmer's profitability depends on renegotiation — which Mondelez has less incentive to do if volumes are down.
who_profits: No clear winner yet. Mondelez is squeezed, not enriched. Competitors (Hershey, Mars, smaller snack makers) face the same cocoa shock, so they're also squeezed. In the near term, whoever holds pricing power and scale wins: large retailers can shift consumer traffic to private label, and large commodity traders who bet on cocoa volatility pocket the spread. Over the longer horizon, winners are likely to be: (1) companies that reformulate away from cocoa (plant-based chocolate, alternative treats) — but that takes time; (2) value brands and private label, which gain share by not fighting the trend; (3) emerging-market-focused snack makers, because Mondelez noted that emerging markets held stronger than developed markets, suggesting local or less-premium brands weathered the shock better. The most direct winner is the cocoa hedge fund or trader who shorted cocoa or went long on cocoa volatility during 2024-2025 — the $2,500-$5,000+ swing is a massive asymmetric bet that paid off.
tension: The core tension is unsustainable: Mondelez depends on cocoa supply that is volatile and geographically concentrated (Ivory Coast and Ghana represent ~70% of global cocoa). Climate change, political risk, and financial speculation will keep hitting supplies in unpredictable spikes. Mondelez can raise prices, but there's a consumer floor — if Oreos at $2.50 become Oreos at $3.50, traffic drops, not because the consumer preference changed, but because the budget constraint tightened. Simultaneously, if Mondelez absorbs the margin hit, shareholders demand stability; if management cuts costs (labor, quality, R&D), the brand weakens over time. The second tension is competitive: if Mondelez holds price and loses volume to private label, market share contracts. If Mondelez cuts price, margins compress further. There is no resolution that restores the 2015-2020 profitability model. The business will shift from premium-growth to cash-return-plus-cost-management, which is what 2026 guidance signals.
surprising_part: The most underappreciated fact is that this isn't management failure. Mondelez's playbook is correct; the operating environment changed. Most CPG companies model elasticity based on 20-year data: if price rises X%, volume drops Y%. Mondelez likely expected -1% to -2% volume for a 5-6% price increase and expected +3-4% net EPS. Instead, -3.7% volume hit despite 4.3% revenue growth, and EPS stayed flat. The surprise is that consumer behavior shifted faster and sharper than historical models predicted. This suggests that lower-income households are now operating under real budget constraints (not just preference), and discretionary spending cuts are happening at the category level, not at the brand level. That's a structural shift, not a cyclical one, and it means Mondelez (and peers) have to rethink the affordability positioning of their brands, not just optimize pricing.
one_sentence: Mondelez's 4.3% revenue growth paired with flat earnings proves that commodity cost pass-through has a consumer affordability ceiling, and Mondelez hit it in 2025.
societal_stake: As commodity volatility becomes structural (climate shocks, supply concentration, financial speculation on inputs), the reliable pass-through mechanism that has fed consumer goods company earnings for 30 years is breaking. Two cascading effects: First, affordable treats become less affordable, shifting snacking from routine habit to planned purchase, which reduces frequency and margins. This hits lower-income households hardest, narrowing access to affordable indulgence. Second, consumer packaged goods companies absorb margin pressure they can't pass through, triggering cost cuts that often come from labor, quality, or brand investment. Over time, that erodes brand strength and makes those companies more vulnerable to private-label competition. The third effect is supply-chain stress: farmers and processors who expected commodity inflation to be passed through now face margin compression, which reduces their investment in supply resilience. The system that worked when commodity spikes were rare and temporary breaks when spikes become frequent and severe.
